facts.raw_span: an 8-month history of a growing, painful tumor on her right buttock
denied experiencing fevers, chills, sweats, weight loss, or malaise
chronic kidney disease
genital herpes simplex virus (HSV)
no history of genital warts, HIV, or inflammatory bowel disease
a 5 × 7-cm verrucous, exophytic tumor with scant yellow drainage on the right medial buttock extending to the perianal skin
Superficial bacterial cultures were obtained from the lesion and grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Microbial cultures were negative for deep fungal infection and acid-fast bacteria
positive for HSV type 2
Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate
Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing plasma cells and focal multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm
Positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells, including multinucleated keratinocytes

concepts.why: The patient presents with a growing, painful tumor on her right buttock, which is described as a 5 × 7-cm verrucous, exophytic tumor with scant yellow drainage, and histology shows hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate.
The patient has a history of genital herpes simplex virus and the lesion is positive for HSV type 2, with positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells.
Superficial bacterial cultures from the lesion grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

The patient presents with a growing, painful tumor on her right buttock, which is described as a 5 × 7-cm verrucous, exophytic tumor with scant yellow drainage, and histology shows hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate, which could be consistent with squamous cell carcinoma.
The patient has a history of genital herpes simplex virus and the lesion is positive for HSV type 2, which could be associated with the development of carcinoma.

concepts.preferred_label: Verrucous carcinoma associated with herpes simplex virus
concepts.why: The presence of multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm and positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells explains the uncovered fact of hematoxylin-eosin stain showing plasma cells and focal multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm.

rationales.F01: The presence of a growing, painful tumor is more typical of a malignant process such as verrucous carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma.
rationales.F04: The patient's history of genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) increases the likelihood of an HSV-related condition, including HSV infection and viral-associated carcinoma.
rationales.F06: The description of the tumor as verrucous and exophytic, with scant yellow drainage, is highly suggestive of a malignant process such as verrucous carcinoma.
rationales.F07: The presence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection is a significant finding that increases the likelihood of an MRSA infection.
rationales.F09: The positive culture for HSV type 2 increases the likelihood of an HSV infection and a viral-associated carcinoma.
rationales.F10: The histological findings of hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate are consistent with a malignant process such as verrucous carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma.
rationales.F11: The presence of plasma cells and focal multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm is consistent with a viral infection and a viral-associated carcinoma.
rationales.F12: The positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells, including multinucleated keratinocytes, is highly suggestive of an HSV infection and a viral-associated carcinoma.
